transfer from 2i/LIF to serum/LIF. Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3). Statistical
significance was determined using a two-tailed t-test (ns, not significant; *P < 0.05; **P
< 0.01; ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001).
3. Although the manuscript establishes a correlation between the presence of
NANOG/WDR5 condensates and transcriptional activation, it does not directly
demonstrate that disruption of these condensates leads to acute suppression of
transcription at target loci. Without such evidence, the causal link between condensate
formation and transcriptional output remains speculative.
We appreciate this insightful comment and have performed additional analyses
and experiments to directly link condensate disruption to acute suppression of nascent
transcription.
First, we re-analysed published nascent RNA-seq data from human SEM leukemia
cells treated with 1,6-hexanediol, generated in the study by Crump et al.1. In this dataset,
we used the nascent RNA samples GSM4141680-GSM4141685 to compare untreated
cells with cells exposed to 1.5% 1,6-hexanediol for 30 min. Differential gene expression
analysis of nascent RNA (edgeR, FDR < 0.05) identified 2,995 up-regulated and 3,454
down-regulated transcripts (Revised Fig. 3A). GO enrichment analysis on the down-
regulated gene set revealed significant enrichment for transcription- and chromatin-
associated terms, including "transcription by RNA polymerase I", "rRNA transcription",
"transcription elongation by RNA polymerase II", and "regulation of chromatin
binding" (Revised Fig. 3B), indicating that short-term 1,6-hexanediol treatment
globally suppresses nascent transcription driven by both RNA polymerases, and
perturbs factors that regulate chromatin binding. In the same gene set, we also observed
significant enrichment for early developmental processes: “in utero embryonic
development”, “blastocyst formation”, and “blastocyst development”. These terms
reflect genes with well-established roles in early embryogenesis and pluripotency-
associated programmes. Together, this independent dataset shows that acute dissolution
of phase-separated nuclear condensates by 1,6-hexanediol rapidly reduces nascent
transcription, with a preferential impact on the transcriptional machinery and early
development /stemness-linked gene programmes.
Second, to test this concept directly in our system, specifically for the WDR5-
NANOG condensates, we used our NANOG R153A knock-in mESCs, in which the
R153A substitution selectively disrupts the WDR5-NANOG interaction and associated
condensate formation. Following a short period of 2i withdrawal, we pulse-labelled
cells with EU and quantified nascent RNA by qPCR at a panel of WDR5/NANOG co-
bound pluripotency and epigenetic regulators (Nanog, Nr5a2, Klf4, Tbx3, Dnmt3a). As
shown in Revised Fig. 3C, nascent transcript levels of all five genes are reduced in
NANOG-R153A cells compared with wild-type controls.
These data provide locus-specific, short-term measurements of nascent
transcription in a genetic background that selectively disrupts WDR5-NANOG
condensate formation. Together with the global nascent RNA-seq analysis of 1,6-
hexanediol-treated SEM cells, they indicate that disruption of phase-separated
condensates, either globally by 1,6-hexanediol or specifically via the WDR5-NANOG
interface, results in rapid repression of nascent transcription, encompassing both
stemness-associated transcriptional programmes and direct WDR5-NANOG target
genes. These findings support a causal link between condensate integrity and
transcriptional output in our system.
Revised Figure 3. Nascent transcription upon condensate disruption.
(A) Volcano plot of nascent RNA-seq from human SEM leukemia cells treated with
1.5% 1,6-hexanediol for 30 min versus untreated controls (GSM4141680-
GSM4141685). Differential expression was assessed with edgeR (FDR < 0.05); red,
up-regulated; blue, down-regulated transcripts, with gene numbers indicated.
(B) GO enrichment of down-regulated nascent transcripts in (A). Bubble plot shows
selected significant terms.
(C) Nascent RNA levels of WDR5/NANOG co-bound pluripotency-related genes in
NANOG WT/R153A mESCs shortly after shifting from 2i/LIF to serum/LIF, measured
by 5-ethynyl uridine (EU) labelling followed by RT-qPCR. Data are shown as fold
change relative to wild-type (mean ± SD, n=3).
4. The manuscript proposes that WDR5 remodels NANOG condensates by acting on
its prion-like C-terminal domain (CTD), yet no domain-specific or loss-of-function
analyses have been conducted to support this model.
To directly address the reviewer’s concern regarding the absence of domain-
specific and loss-of-function evidence supporting our model, we performed two
additional experiments:
First, we purified the N-terminal region of NANOG (GFP-NANOG 1-155), which
lacks the CTD, and tested its ability to phase separate in vitro. This truncated construct
failed to form detectable condensates even under crowding conditions (10% PEG8000),
supporting the necessity of the CTD for condensate formation (Revised Fig. 4A and
Supplementary Fig. 1h).
Second, we performed Thioflavin-T (ThT) kinetic assays to assess the formation
of β-sheet-enriched aggregates, comparing wild-type NANOG and a CTD mutant
(W8A) previously shown to impair self-association2. As shown in Revised Fig. 4B,
NANOGW8A markedly attenuated ThT fluorescence relative to NANOGWT, indicating
that the CTD contributes to the formation of β-sheet-enriched aggregates. Addition of
WDR5WT suppressed the ThT signal of NANOGWT, whereas the WIN-site mutant
WDR5F133A exhibited a weaker effect, consistent with our structural data showing that
the WIN motif serves as a key interface mediating the WDR5-NANOG interaction.
Together, these domain-specific and loss-of-function data, including CTD
truncation, CTD point mutation, and differential response to WDR5WT versus
WDR5F133A, provide direct experimental support for the model in which WDR5
modulates the biophysical state of NANOG condensates by engaging the homeodomain
and sterically constraining the CTD, thereby limiting its assembly into β-sheet-enriched
aggregates. We have added these new results to the revised manuscript (Fig. 3h and
Supplementary Fig. 1h).
Revised Figure 4. Mechanistic assays dissecting NANOG assembly and its
modulation by WDR5.
(A) In vitro droplet formation of 20 μM GFP-NANOG 1-155 under the indicated
PEG8000 concentrations (0, 5, 10%). Assays were performed in 25 mM Tris-HCl (pH
8.0) and 150 mM NaCl. Scale bars, 10 μm.
(B) ThT aggregation kinetics of full length NANOGWT alone, NANOGWT + WDR5WT,
NANOGWT + WDR5F133A, and NANOGW8A; Buffer + ThT serves as control. Traces
show normalized ThT fluorescence over time (mean ± SD, n = 3).
5. The reported Rmerge value for the X-ray diffraction data appears high. The authors
should verify the accuracy of the data processing and clarify whether this value reflects
issues in data quality or resolution-dependent artifacts.
In the original “Data collection” line, we inadvertently reported the integration
range (50.00-1.78 Å). During data processing, we applied a resolution cutoff at 2.50 Å,
because the outer-shell I/σI fell below 2.0, which is the classical signal-to-noise cut-off
for usable reflections3. The structure was therefore refined using the 50.0-2.50 Å dataset.
We have corrected Table 1 to accurately reflect 50.0-2.50 Å. We thank the reviewer for
prompting us to re-examine the processing parameters and present the limits
unambiguously.
For the same dataset, HKL2000 (truncated at 2.50 Å) scaling yielded: overall
R =0.179, R =0.193, R =0.073 (outer shell: R =0.650, R =0.703,

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This study reports a direct interaction between the Nanog homeodomain, otherwise
involved in DNA binding, with the WDR5 co-regulator using X-ray crystallography
further verified via NMR. This interaction affects formation of LLPS, genome-wide
binding profiles, and cancer stemness as shown with a structure-informed R153A
mutation. They propose that WDR5 induced a structural switch of Nanog aggregates
from inactive prion-like forms towards active liquid-like forms. This is a bold and
intriguing claim with a profound impact on the field of transcription factor biology. This
reviewer is not fully convinced that the data presented in past and present papers
support such a far-reaching claim. I find this is an important study with high-quality
data, but I feel some of the interpretations go too far and require a major revision and
down-toning of the proposed amyloid to LLPS switch unless very compelling new data
are added.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for his/her thoughtful and constructive evaluation.
In response to these concerns, we have implemented a series of focused revisions.
(1) We removed the phrase “prion-like to LLPS switch” and replaced all references
to “prion-like” with a more accurate description of NANOG-alone assemblies as β-
sheet-enriched, irregular aggregates.
(2) We incorporated an orthogonal ThT kinetics assay comparing NANOGWT,
NANOGW8A, NANOGWT + WDR5WT, and NANOGWT + WDR5F133A (see our Response
to Reviewer 1.4). This experiment further validates the role of NANOG’s C-terminal
domain (CTD) in the formation of β-sheet-enriched aggregates, while also revealing
how WDR5 modulates the condensate state.
(3) We performed additional EMSA and phase separation assays to clarify how
WDR5 influences NANOG-DNA engagement, showing that WDR5 modulates
NANOG’s DNA-binding behavior in a context- and concentration-dependent manner.
(4) We performed additional EB differentiation assays using R153A ESC lines and
clarified our rationale for incorporating leukemia stem cells (LSCs) to assess whether
the WDR5-NANOG regulatory axis operates in a transcriptionally plastic, disease-
relevant context.
Together, we address the reviewer’s concerns by refining structural terminology,
introducing orthogonal experimental support, and sharpening the mechanistic narrative.
The point-by-point revision response is listed as follows.
Major Strengths:
Linking the molecular details of how chromatin regulators work together at atomic
resolution with their operation in the nucleus to regulate genes and cell behavior is of
paramount importance, and I applaud the authors for taking this holistic approach. The
experimental content and the breadth of methods (NMR, X-ray, EM, LLPS, and several
cell-based and in vivo analyses) are impressive.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and encouraging comments on
our study.
Key Limitations and Recommendations for Revision:
1. The authors claim that WDR5 switches Nanog’s functionally inert prion-like state to
a transactivating LLPS state. However, their cryo-EM analysis does not appear to
clearly reveal a prion-like state. The previous NCB paper that first claimed the prion
character of Nanog is very interesting, but it did not contain a structure or data for prion-
like seeding or templating. Protease resistance was also not shown there. Could authors
visualise the amyloids via cryo-EM? As of now, it seems the prion-like behaviour of
Nanog is a hypothesis from with indirect support from fibrous aggregate morphology
and beta-richness alone? Is there any evidence that the fibrillar state authors report in
Figures 1 and 4 represent bona fide amyloids with beta structures (refer to work by
Ruben Hervas and Ryskeldi-Falcon labs and others for structural work on amyloids to
provide ultimate evidence)?
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. We agree that our current data do not
demonstrate bona fide amyloid fibrils in the strict structural sense. Accordingly, we
have revised the manuscript to adopt more conservative terminology (e.g., “β-sheet-
enriched, irregular aggregates”) and removed the phrase “prion-like to LLPS switch”
throughout the text to avoid overinterpretation.
Our original use of the term “prion-like” was based on Choi et al.2, who proposed
that NANOG undergoes prion-like assembly and gelation. However, as the reviewer
astutely noted, that study did not provide direct evidence of templated seeding, protease
resistance, or a cross-β ultrastructure. With this important clarification in mind, and
upon re-evaluating both the literature and our own data, we now describe NANOG-
alone assemblies as β-sheet-enriched, irregular aggregates rather than prion-like or
amyloid in nature. As noted in the manuscript, we originally employed negative-stain
EM to visualize the morphological transition of NANOG upon WDR5 binding.
While
NANOG alone formed irregular, amorphous aggregates, co-incubation with WDR5
induced droplet-like structures exhibiting features consistent with LLPS (Fig. 1b, c).
However, we have not conducted cryo-EM under optimized fibrillization conditions to
characterize the molecular architecture of these assemblies. We are interested in this
direction and view it as an important future extension.
Consistent with the scope of this study, our mechanistic focus is not on defining
the ultrastructure of the aggregates, but rather on demonstrating that WDR5 binding
suppresses aggregation and promotes a dynamic, liquid-like condensate state, which in
turn enhances chromatin association and transcriptional activity. To strengthen this
interpretation, we have incorporated an orthogonal readout of β-sheet assembly using
ThT kinetics (Revised Fig. 4B, see our Response to Reviewer 1.4). Comparing
NANOGWT, NANOGW8A, and NANOGWT in the presence of WDR5WT or the WIN-
deficient F133A mutant, we observed that ThT signal increases for NANOG alone but
is significantly reduced upon WDR5WT binding; this effect is attenuated with the F133A
mutant. These findings directly support our model without overinterpreting the
aggregates as bona fide amyloids.
In summary, we refined the terminology, added orthogonal ThT-based evidence
that WDR5 suppresses β-sheet-enriched aggregation, and explicitly bounded our claims.
The revised manuscript now frames WDR5 as a modulator of the NANOG condensate
state, rather than as the driver of an amyloid-to-LLPS switch.
2. Authors fail to elaborate on how WDR5 affects Nanog's DNA binding. Questions
that come to mind: Can DNA/WDR/Nanog form a ternary complex? Or does the
Nanog-WDR5 interaction block DNA binding? Does a mutation that disrupts WDR5
interaction not also impede DNA binding? The proposed mechanism is not clear and
should, in my opinion, be resolved before publication in a high-visibility journal.
Authors are experts in quantitative molecular binding assays and have a battery of
proteins at their disposal, so I do not see why they couldn’t, with reasonable effort,
study how WDR5 affects Nanog’s DNA interaction.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. We agree that understanding how WDR5
modulates NANOG’s DNA-binding behavior is mechanistically relevant to our study.
In response, we have performed additional experiments, now included as
Supplementary Fig. 5a-c, to assess whether WDR5 affects NANOG-DNA interactions.
To assess potential structural compatibility between WDR5 and DNA on NANOG,
we aligned the crystal structure of the WDR5-NANOG HD complex with the model of
NANOG HD bound to DNA, based on the published NANOG-DNA structure (PDB:
4RBO). The alignment revealed a steric clash between WDR5 and the DNA duplex at
the canonical recognition helix of NANOG HD, indicating that WDR5 binding and
DNA binding likely compete for the same interface (Revised Fig. 5A).
To test this hypothesis experimentally, we performed electrophoretic mobility shift
assays (EMSA) using fluorescently labeled NANOG target DNA (Tcf3-DNA) and
increasing concentrations of WDR5. These assays were carried out under low-salt
conditions to enhance NANOG-DNA binding affinity and enable detection at lower
protein concentrations (Revised Fig. 5B). This helped minimize aggregation and well
retention artifacts often observed at high concentrations, especially in the presence of
excess WDR5. We observed that WDR5 progressively disrupted NANOG-DNA
complex formation in a dose-dependent manner (Revised Fig. 5B), supporting a
competitive binding model in which WDR5 modulates NANOG’s DNA association by
occupying overlapping surfaces on the homeodomain.
Interestingly, under molecular crowding conditions, we observed that WDR5,
NANOG, and DNA co-partition into tripartite phase-separated condensates (Revised
Fig. 5C), despite the apparent steric conflict at the atomic interface between WDR5 and
DNA that prevents NANOG binding. This observation suggests that while WDR5
binding and DNA binding to NANOG are mutually exclusive in a strict structural
context, they can nonetheless coexist within higher-order condensates, likely through
multivalent, dynamic interactions. This co-condensation is likely concentration-
dependent and may be facilitated by the dynamic assembly properties of phase-
separated condensates, which can accommodate partial competition between individual
binding events through multivalent interactions. Such behavior is consistent with recent
findings that transcription factors, coactivators, and DNA can co-enrich within the same
transcriptional condensates6,7.
Moreover, as shown in our original Supplementary Fig. 5d-e, the R153A mutation,
which disrupts the WDR5-NANOG interaction, does not impair NANOG’s DNA-
binding capability, as confirmed by both EMSA and fluorescence polarization assays.
This finding further supports the specificity of the WDR5 effect and excludes the
possibility that loss of DNA binding accounts for the observed phenotypes in the mutant.
Taken together, these data indicate that WDR5 modulates NANOG’s DNA-
binding behavior in a context- and concentration-dependent manner, likely by shifting
the equilibrium between WDR5-bound and DNA-bound states of NANOG. We have
incorporated these new data into Supplementary Fig. 5a-c and added a corresponding
explanation in the Results section.
Revised Figure 5. WDR5 modulates NANOG-DNA binding.
(A) Structural superimposition of the NANOG HD-WDR5 complex and the NANOG
HD-Tcf3 DNA complex (PDB: 4RBO) reveals overlapping binding interfaces on the
NANOG homeodomain.
(B) EMSA showing the concentration of NANOG HD required for complete binding
to Tcf3 DNA (left, 1 nM DNA with increasing NANOG HD). Based on these results,
the right panel assesses competitive inhibition by titrating WDR5 (0-320 nM) into pre-
mixed samples containing 40 nM NANOG HD and 1 nM DNA. All assays were
performed in buffer containing 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.8), 50 mM KCl, 10 mM NaCl,
and 10% glycerol.
(C) Representative fluorescence microscopy images showing the formation of phase-
separated condensates in ternary mixtures of GFP-NANOG, WDR5-RFP, and AMCA-
labeled Tcf3 DNA at defined molar ratios of 1:3:1 and 1:4:1. Droplet assays were
performed in buffer containing 25 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, and 5%
PEG8000. Scale bars, 10 μm.
3. The Nanog R153A ESC lines provide a powerful tool that I felt was underused. Why
was stemness and pluripotency not further examined using this line (rather than with
cancer stem cells)? It would be interesting to study differentiation potential, EB
formation, and (optionally) developmental potential in vivo.
We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we expanded
our analyses using embryoid body (EB) differentiation assays, while retaining the
leukemia stem-cell (LSC) model to assess whether the WDR5-NANOG regulatory axis
extends to a disease-relevant, pathological stem-like state.
We examined LSCs alongside ESCs to test whether the WDR5-NANOG
regulatory mechanism is conserved beyond early development and functions in
pathological stemness. This extension is grounded in both biological and translational
rationale. Biologically, NANOG and WDR5 are aberrantly expressed or functionally
repurposed in multiple malignancies, where they support plastic, stem-like
transcriptional programmes; Thus, a condensate-based regulatory mechanism defined
in ESCs could plausibly apply in cancer. Translationally, C16 is a WDR5 WIN-site
probe developed and characterized in leukemic systems, making LSCs the most
relevant context to assess whether pharmacologic disruption of the WDR5-NANOG
interface can blunt malignant self-renewal. In this framework, ESCs offer precise
mechanistic dissection, while LSCs provide pathophysiological context and therapeutic
relevance.
As suggested by the reviewer, we performed EB differentiation assays to further
examine the impact of the WDR5-NANOG interaction on early lineage specification.
As shown in Revised Fig. 6, during EB differentiation, R153A mutant cells displayed
increased expression of somatic lineage markers (Fgf5, Gata4, Gata6, Nestin) relative
to WT cells. Conversely, the expression of primordial germ cells (PGC) markers
(Prdm14, Prdm1, Nanos) is reduced, aligning with previous findings that NANOG is
required for maintaining pluripotency while also facilitating PGC specification8. We
have incorporated these new data into Supplementary Fig. 6b.
We agree that in vivo developmental assays would further strengthen our
conclusions and represent an important direction for future investigation. However, due
to current limitations in time and resources, such experiments are beyond the scope of
the present study. We view these studies as a key direction for future research and are
committed to pursuing them using appropriately designed models.
Revised Figure6. EB differentiation of NANOG WT and R153A lines.
Quantitative RT-PCR analysis of pluripotency/PGC markers (A) and somatic lineage
markers (B) in ESCs and EBs derived from isogenic NANOG WT and R153A lines.
Data are mean ± SD (n = 3), normalized to actin and plotted relative to ESC WT.
Statistical significance was determined using a two-tailed t-test (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01,
***P < 0.001). T is also known as Brachyury.
Minor comments:
4. How does 1,6-hexanediol treatment affect ESC viability, morphology and self-
renewal?
Under our experimental conditions (3% 1,6-hexanediol for 15 minutes), we
observed no appreciable changes in ESC morphology or viability, as shown in the
Revised Fig. 7. These results indicate that the treatment is acutely well tolerated and
does not induce overt cytotoxicity.
We did not assess long-term self-renewal, as the purpose of this perturbation was
to probe the biophysical sensitivity of WDR5-NANOG condensates rather than their
functional consequences on self-renewal. Nonetheless, the absence of acute toxicity
supports the validity of our interpretation. Similar concentrations and exposure
durations of 1,6-hexanediol have been widely used in ESCs and other mammalian
systems to transiently disrupt phase-separated compartments without compromising
cell integrity6,9.
Revised Figure 7. Short-term 1,6-hexanediol treatment in ESCs.
(A) Phase-contrast images of ESC colonies under untreated control conditions (MOCK)
or after treatment with 3% 1,6-hexanediol (1,6-HD) for 15 min.
(B) Quantification of ESC viability after MOCK or 3% 1,6-HD treatment for 15 min,
expressed as percentage of control. Data represent mean ± SD (n = 3); ns, not significant
(unpaired t-test).
5. For easier cross-referencing, I recommend adding conventional HD numbering to
key residues (i.e. Q50, N51)
In Figure 2 or 3, please include the sequence of the Nanog HD with annotated helices,
DNA binding residues (Q50, N51), and mark those subject to mutational analysis. There
is an alignment in the supplement that could be modified and moved to the main text.
To address this comment, we have updated Figure 2 in the revised manuscript to
show the sequence of the NANOG HD with annotated helices and conventional
homeodomain numbering, and highlights conserved base-specific DNA-contacting
residues, including Q50 and N51, as blue dots (Fig. 2d). The multiple sequence
alignment that was previously presented in Supplementary Fig. 3e has been moved to
Fig. 2d to improve accessibility. The residues subjected to mutational analysis in this
study were designed later, based on structural insights from the WDR5-NANOG
complex, and are first introduced in the corresponding structural figures. Nevertheless,
this alignment provides a useful reference for mapping these mutants onto the
homeodomain.
6. The x-ray structure of Nanog was resolved in apo and DNA-bound forms. Why did
authors use structural modelling rather than these experimental structures for some of
their analysis?
We agree that the available apo and DNA-bound crystal structures of the NANOG
homeodomain provide valuable structural information. Our original use of a predicted
model in Supplementary Fig. 3a was intended to visualize the flexible loop region
(residues 96-104), which is not resolved in the available experimental structures due to
disorder but is predicted to contribute to the WDR5-binding surface.
In accordance with the reviewer’s suggestion, we have now replaced the model in
Supplementary Fig. 3a with the experimentally determined structure of the NANOG
homeodomain (PDB: 2VI6). The flexible loop spanning residues 96-104, which is not
resolved in the crystal structure, is indicated by a dashed line to represent its disordered
conformation.
We also performed a structural alignment between the DNA-bound NANOG
homeodomain (PDB: 4RBO) and our WDR5-NANOG complex. This alignment is now
included in Supplementary Fig. 5a to illustrate the spatial relationship between the
DNA-binding surface and the WDR5-binding region.
7. Please compare DNA motifs bound by Nanog and the R153A mutant. Does it affect
preferences for the TAATGG like HD motif. Does the mutant alter the otherwise often
seen co-occupancy of loci by Nanog, Sox2 and Oct4?
Figure S6: Does the motif utilization change in shared and Nanog/mutant unique
peaks?
We thank the reviewer for the insightful question. We performed motif enrichment
analysis using HOMER (q-value ≤ 1×10⁻³) on NANOGWT and NANOGR153A ChIP-seq
datasets, and functionally categorized all significant motifs based on established
transcription factor families. As shown in Revised Fig. 8A, most motifs (208) are shared
between the two datasets, while 56 and 12 motifs are uniquely identified in NANOGWT-
only and NANOGR153A-only regions, respectively.
Motif composition analysis reveals that shared binding sites are predominantly
enriched for NANOG-associated transcriptional programmes, including the TAAT-
containing HD motif and the pluripotency core module characteristic of NANOG-
SOX2-OCT4 co-occupancy (Revised Fig. 8B). In contrast, NANOGWT-unique and
NANOGR153A-unique regions contain relatively fewer motifs, most of which fall into
uncharacterized or noncanonical categories (Revised Fig. 8B). These results suggest
that the R153A mutation does not redirect NANOG binding toward alternative
transcriptional modules.
Revised Figure 8. Motif utilization in NANOG WT and R153A peaks.
(A) Number of significant motifs identified in NANOGWT-unique, shared, and
NANOGR153A-unique peaks (HOMER known-motif enrichment, Benjamini-Hochberg
q ≤ 1×10⁻³).
(B) Heatmap showing the distribution of enriched motifs grouped by functional
categories. Color scale represents motif counts; numbers within cells indicate the count
per category.
8. The Nanog-DNA Kd’s in Figure S5 are a lot lower (1000x?) thn previously reported.
Whilst many parameters can affect binding affinity this difference looks very drastic.
Please ensure titrations are not performed with [DNA]>=[Kd] when reliable Kd’s are
aspired. I recommend following these very useful guidelines:
https://elifesciences.org/articles/57264
We thank the reviewer for the expert comment regarding Kd determination. As
stated in the original Methods section, our fluorescence polarization (FP) experiments
were performed using 25 mM HEPES (pH 7.8), 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, and
25 nM 5′-FAM-labeled Tcf3 DNA (acctgttaatgggagcgc). Under these physiological-salt
conditions, the fitted Kd for wild type NANOG HD was approximately 1.9 µM
(Supplementary Fig. 5d), and consistent results were obtained from parallel EMSA
assays (Supplementary Fig. 5e).
Prior reports span a broad range of affinities owing to differences in construct
design, DNA sequence, and buffer composition. For example, Jauch et al.10reported an
apparent Kd of ~26 nM under low-salt conditions (10 mM HEPES, 50 mM KCl,
10 mM NaCl), whereas Hayashi et al.11 reported a Kd of ~5.9 µM for wild-type human
NANOG HD binding to a biotinylated OCT4 promoter sequence under higher salt and
more stringent conditions. Thus, our measured Kd values in the low micromolar range
are consistent with these prior studies, considering differences in buffer composition,
DNA sequence, and assay format.
To explicitly evaluate the impact of ionic strength, we additionally performed a
low-salt EMSA (10 mM HEPES, 50 mM KCl, 10 mM NaCl; 1 nM Tcf3 DNA) in the
Revised Fig. 5B. Titration of NANOG HD under these conditions yielded an apparent
Kd of ~20-40 nM, closely matching the magnitude reported by Jauch et al. This direct
comparison confirms that the large shift relative to our FP value primarily reflects the
expected ionic-strength dependence of electrostatic DNA binding, rather than
differences in assay quality or analysis.
Importantly, as the reviewer noted, accurate Kd determination requires the
condition [DNA] ≪ Kd. Our assays used 25 nM DNA, more than 75-fold below the
fitted Kd (~1.9 µM) under physiological-salt conditions, and the low-salt EMSA used
1 nM DNA versus a 20-40 nM Kd (≥20-fold lower), both within recommended bounds.
We have reiterated the relevant concentration ranges in the revised figure legends and
Methods to ensure transparency and reproducibility.
9. Similar amorphous aggregates were reported for other pluripotency factors; this
could be discussed.
We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. Indeed, in addition to
classical liquid-like condensates, recent studies have reported that several pluripotency
transcription factors can also adopt less dynamic or amorphous assemblies under
defined conditions. For example, SOX2 has been shown to form amorphous aggregates
over time in vitro rather than maintaining a spherical droplet12. Similarly, MYC has
been reported to form stress-induced multimers13 and undergo sequence-dependent
reductions in condensate dynamics, culminating in irreversible aggregation14.
These findings raise the possibility that transcription factors involved in
pluripotency regulation may share a common capacity to transition between distinct
material states, ranging from dynamic condensates to less fluid or aggregated
assemblies. Such regulated modulation of material properties may serve as a general
mechanism to coordinate genome organization and transcriptional output.
In this context, the β-sheet-enriched aggregates we observe for NANOG and their
remodeling by WDR5 may reflect a more generalizable strategy by which cofactor
interactions modulate the material properties of transcription factors to affect chromatin
occupancy and gene regulation. We have expanded the Discussion to include this
perspective, proposing that regulated transitions in transcription factor condensate state
may be a broadly conserved mechanism for pluripotency maintenance and genome
control.
10. They also tested the disruption of NANOG and WDR5 interaction in LSCs,
drug group (C16) and DMSO control. I wonder if they treat healthy stem cells (ESCs,
MSCs, et al) with C16. The switch to LSCs looks a bit abrupt and inconsistent with the
rest of the study. Please comment/explain.
We thank the reviewer for the opportunity to clarify the scope of our
pharmacological experiments. As noted in our response to Comment 3, we used ESCs
to mechanistically dissect the WDR5-NANOG interaction through a targeted genetic
perturbation (NANOG R153A). This approach allowed us to isolate the effects of
disrupting this specific interface without introducing the broader network-level
perturbations that small molecules might cause in pluripotent cells.
In contrast, we evaluated pharmacologic inhibition using C16, a WIN site
antagonist of WDR5 originally developed and validated in AML models. Accordingly,
we performed these experiments in LSCs, which provide a disease-relevant context to
assess on-target activity and therapeutic relevance. For this reason, we did not apply
C16 to ESCs or MSCs in the present study. We did, however, include normal
hematopoietic progenitors (HSPCs) as a functional control. Notably, C16 induced only
modest changes in CFU output from HSPCs at concentrations that robustly suppressed
AE9a LSC colony formation (Fig. 6b), suggesting a degree of selectivity in a
therapeutically relevant context.
11. The LLPS shown in Figures 1 and 4 had very high protein concentrations, which
may not reflect the real physiological concentrations experienced in the cell. Would
phenomena persist if changed to use a more physiological concentration of NANOG
and WDR5 in vitro?
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. It is a well-established and
broadly accepted principle in LLPS research that protein concentrations used in in vitro
assays often exceed average physiological levels. This methodological choice is not
only widely recognized but also practically necessary, as simplified reconstitution
systems lack critical cellular components such as macromolecular crowding, chromatin
scaffolds, and multivalent cofactors like RNA and transcriptional coactivators, all of
which are known to significantly lower the saturation concentration (C ) required for
sat
condensate formation. As discussed by Alberti et al15, increasing protein concentrations
in vitro can help compensate for the absence of these phase-promoting factors.
Consequently, the use of micromolar concentrations of proteins is a standard practice
in LLPS studies.
In the context of transcription factors, Morin et al.16 reported that KLF4 forms
liquid-like condensates at physiological salt and pH, but only above ~1.0 µM in the
absence of DNA, a concentration that exceeds its estimated nuclear abundance. At the
same time, the addition of λ-DNA triggers foci formation below the bulk C ,
sat
illustrating how DNA scaffolds can significantly lower the condensation threshold.
Similarly, Boija et al.7 demonstrated that a range of transcription factors, including
OCT4, MYC, SOX2, and RARα, form condensates in vitro at concentrations of 10-40
µM. Sabari et al6 observed BRD4-IDR and MED1-IDR condensates at concentrations
of 5-20 µM. These examples collectively support that micromolar concentrations are
typical for in vitro LLPS studies of transcriptional regulators. Our use of 20 µM
NANOG and 20-80 µM WDR5 is therefore well within the established experimental
range and methodologically consistent with prior work. Importantly, our core
conclusions do not depend on the absolute concentration thresholds required to initiate
LLPS, but rather on the consistent and reproducible effect of WDR5 in modulating the
material properties of NANOG condensates under matched experimental conditions.
In addition to the in vitro evidence, our in vivo experiments further support the
biological relevance of WDR5-NANOG condensates. We observed that endogenous
NANOG and WDR5 colocalize within nuclear puncta displaying hallmarks of phase-
separated condensates, including sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol and dynamic molecular
exchange. These condensates showed WDR5-dependent changes in biophysical
properties and chromatin occupancy, consistent with the modulatory effects
characterized in vitro. Together, these results provide complementary in vitro and in
vivo evidence that WDR5 regulates NANOG's phase behavior in a physiologically
meaningful manner.
12. The FRAP of Figure 1H does not seem to recover too much after adding WDR5.
Please comment/explain.
We appreciate the reviewer’s observation. While FRAP recovery in Figure 1h is
increased when NANOG is co-expressed with WDR5, we acknowledge that the extent
of this increase may appear modest by visual inspection.
Biologically, partial and relatively slow FRAP recovery is often observed in vivo
for transcription-related condensates, even when they are functional. This phenomenon
is well documented and reflects the presence of a substantial immobile fraction arising
from chromatin tethering and the viscoelastic nature of the nuclear environment17.
In our case, although the absolute extent of recovery is not dramatic, it is
consistently higher with WDR5 co-expression than with NANOG alone. Together with
our in vitro FRAP results (Fig. 1j and 1l), which show more pronounced recovery under
controlled conditions, these findings support the conclusion that WDR5 enhances the
dynamic exchange of NANOG molecules, even though a chromatin-tethered fraction
likely remains immobile in vivo. We believe this shift is mechanistically meaningful
and consistent with the behavior of other transcriptional condensates.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: All issues have been addressed. I recommend acceptance for publication.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I co-reviewed this paper with an ECR in my team. A regulated switch between prion and LLPS state driven by WDR would be fascinating but requires more structural evidence, which the authors acknowledge. The authors have added assays to support the claim that WDR5 can nudge NANOG into undergo liquid-liquid phase separation and to regulate stem cell transcription. The newly added assays, such as Co-IP, ChIP-qPCR, a sequential differentiation assay, and re-analysis of RNA/ChIP-seq data, support the rational use of C16, the direct cause of epigenetic changes, and transcriptional activation by the WDR5/NANOG LLPS. The newly added EMSA/LLPS show that WDR5 competes with DNA for NANOG interactions.
I remain a bit puzzled as to the main mechanistic model and would encourage the authors to further clarify the graphical summary and the key narrative. I note that a WDR5/NANOG appears – at least in 1-to-1 stoichiometry, incompatible with DNA binding – yet, WDR5 binding to NANOG facilitates its binding to target genes. It would be nice if this could be reconciled/explained. We recommend acceptance of this fascinating study with only minor remaining suggestions:
• In Figure 1g, please circle where you bleached to make it more straightforward.
• ChIP-qPCR only has 3 technical analyses. Any possible independent replicates?
• Please ensure statistical analysis is clarified in all legends and relevant methods sections
• Please clarify the independent replication (not just repeat recordings) of the new THT fluorescence assay and briefly explain its principle (possibly with a small cartoon next to the data figure).
• I am still confused as to the main model how WDR5 helps promote the binding of NANOG to its target genes when EMSAs suggest WDR5 prevents the HD from binding DNA. I cannot follow the explanations the authors provide for these observations in the main text. Along these lines: If the WDR5 competes with NANOG for binding DNA, why would a mutation (R153A), which reduces WDR but not DNA binding, result in a lot less binding intensity (Figure 5A)?
• I find the graphical summary in Fig. hard to read and struggle to link the legend to the displayed items. Could this be less convoluted and more concise?

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-by-Point Responses to Reviewers' Comments
REVIEWERS' COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
All issues have been addressed. I recommend acceptance for publication.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive comments and support.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this paper with an ECR in my team. A regulated switch between prion
and LLPS state driven by WDR would be fascinating but requires more structural
evidence, which the authors acknowledge. The authors have added assays to support
the claim that WDR5 can nudge NANOG into undergo liquid-liquid phase separation
and to regulate stem cell transcription. The newly added assays, such as Co-IP, ChIP-
qPCR, a sequential differentiation assay, and re-analysis of RNA/ChIP-seq data,
support the rational use of C16, the direct cause of epigenetic changes, and
transcriptional activation by the WDR5/NANOG LLPS. The newly added
EMSA/LLPS show that WDR5 competes with DNA for NANOG interactions. I remain
a bit puzzled as to the main mechanistic model and would encourage the authors to
further clarify the graphical summary and the key narrative. I note that a
WDR5/NANOG appears – at least in 1-to-1 stoichiometry, incompatible with DNA
binding – yet, WDR5 binding to NANOG facilitates its binding to target genes. It would
be nice if this could be reconciled/explained. We recommend acceptance of this
fascinating study with only minor remaining suggestions:
We thank the reviewer and the co-reviewer for their careful evaluation and are
grateful for their positive recommendation. Regarding the reviewer’s inquiry about the
mechanistic model and the compatibility of WDR5/DNA binding, we have provided a
detailed discussion and reconciliation of these observations in our response to the
specific comment below. We have also revised the graphical summary (Fig. 7) to clarify
this dynamic mechanism as suggested.
• In Figure 1g, please circle where you bleached to make it more straightforward.
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have now more clearly marked the
bleached regions in Fig. 1g by using thicker white dashed circles.
• ChIP-qPCR only has 3 technical analyses. Any possible independent replicates?
We thank the reviewer for this question and apologize for any ambiguity in our
previous description. We would like to clarify that the ChIP-qPCR experiments were
performed using three independent replicates. Specifically, for each genotype
(NANOGWT and NANOGR153A), we carried out the time-resolved differentiation assay
independently in three separate mESC cultures, and the samples at each time point were
harvested and processed independently through chromatin preparation. Thus, the data
points represent independent replicates, not technical qPCR repeats from a single
extraction, and statistical testing was performed across these independent replicates.
We have updated the figure legend to state this explicitly.
• Please ensure statistical analysis is clarified in all legends and relevant methods
sections.
We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. In line with Nature
Communications’ statistical reporting guidance, we have systematically revised all
figure legends and the relevant methods sections to provide complete information on
the statistical analyses.
• Please clarify the independent replication (not just repeat recordings) of the new THT
fluorescence assay and briefly explain its principle (possibly with a small cartoon next
to the data figure).
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. We have now clarified in the legend
to Fig. 3h that the ThT fluorescence assay was performed as three independent ThT
experiments. In addition, we have expanded the methods section to briefly describe the
assay principle, stating that ThT is a fluorescent dye whose emission increases upon
binding to β-sheet-enriched protein assemblies and therefore reports on the aggregation
state of NANOG. Given the well-established nature of this assay, we believe this textual
description effectively clarifies the principle.
• I am still confused as to the main model how WDR5 helps promote the binding of
NANOG to its target genes when EMSAs suggest WDR5 prevents the HD from binding
DNA. I cannot follow the explanations the authors provide for these observations in the
main text. Along these lines: If the WDR5 competes with NANOG for binding DNA,
why would a mutation (R153A), which reduces WDR but not DNA binding, result in a
lot less binding intensity (Figure 5A)?
We thank the reviewer for the opportunity to clarify this point. The EMSA assay
isolates a minimal system with purified NANOG HD and short DNA probes to directly
assess NANOG HD-DNA binding. This setup addresses two specific questions:
whether the R153A substitution alters the intrinsic NANOG HD-DNA interaction, and
whether WDR5 binding is compatible with NANOG HD-DNA binding in this
simplified in vitro context.
In the nucleus, however, the functional outcome depends critically on the assembly
state of NANOG within the complex chromatin environment. Our data indicate that, in
the absence of WDR5, NANOG tends to form β-sheet-enriched, slowly exchanging
assemblies driven by its C-terminal region. We therefore infer that the R153A mutant,
which impairs WDR5 binding, functionally mimics this "NANOG-alone" state and is
prone to forming non-productive aggregates that are less available for productive
chromatin engagement. This can explain why R153A exhibits reduced ChIP-seq signals
despite intact HD-DNA binding.
In the presence of WDR5, we propose that NANOG is remodeled into dynamic,
liquid-like condensates. Within these condensates, the high local concentration of
soluble NANOG and the multivalent nature of the assembly are expected to overcome
the direct steric competition observed under dilute EMSA conditions. Instead of a rigid,
permanent WDR5-NANOG-DNA ternary complex, NANOG-WDR5 association and
NANOG-DNA engagement can proceed via a dynamic exchange mechanism in which
NANOG transiently dissociates from WDR5 to engage high-affinity DNA motifs and
then re-engages WDR5 and other cofactors. Furthermore, WDR5 acts as a scaffold to
co-recruit MOF and MLL complexes, establishing a permissive chromatin environment
that further stabilizes NANOG occupancy at pluripotency-associated promoters.
Consistent with this view, our ternary LLPS experiment shows that NANOG,
WDR5,
and DNA can co-partition into the same phase-separated droplets. We have revised the
graphical summary and figure legend of Fig. 7 to present this mechanism more clearly.
• I find the graphical summary in Fig. hard to read and struggle to link the legend to the
displayed items. Could this be less convoluted and more concise?
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. In response, we have revised Fig. 7 to
make the graphical summary less convoluted and easier to follow.
1. We simplified the visual design by removing distracting details and focusing
the schematic on the two key NANOG assembly states highlighted in our study—an
aggregate-like, less dynamic state (upper/lower panels) versus a WDR5-associated,
